title: Visual pathway
prompt:
Create a 32-second silent English 1920×1080 educational animation about Visual pathway for Introduction to Neuroscience.
Use Remotion 4.0.410, React 19 and the introduction-to-neuroscience course kit. Reproduce the actual video in assets/source-kits/introduction-to-neuroscience/src/videos/ns07-visual-pathway.tsx; fps is 30.
Keep the same dark course palette and diagrams. Use the actual state transitions from the source, not a generic neural-network animation.

Scene plan:
1. 0–6s, hemifield: Light-ray guides connect the left target to the right half of each retinal diagram: left-eye nasal retina and right-eye temporal retina. These two retinal patches receive paired signal markers. Why: Optical inversion places left-field information on right retinal halves in both eyes. Visible result: The two activated retinal patches have different nasal/temporal identities despite carrying the same left-field target.
2. 6–11s, optic: Two distinguishable packets travel down their respective optic nerves and stop before the chiasm; inactive fibers remain as faint context. Why: Each eye initially sends its retinal signals through its own optic nerve. Visible result: Two separate packets reach the chiasm from different eyes; neither has switched side yet.
3. 11–20s, chiasm: The nasal packet curves across the midline into the right optic tract; the temporal packet follows its outer ipsilateral path. Both finish on the right, side by side rather than fusing. Why: Only nasal retinal fibers decussate; temporal fibers remain ipsilateral. Visible result: The crossing packet passes the midline and the temporal packet never does; both contribute to the same right tract.
4. 20–27s, thalamus: Incoming markers terminate at the LGN relay and outgoing activity progresses along right optic radiations, then reaches the right occipital endpoint. Why: The main conscious visual pathway relays in the LGN before visual cortex. Visible result: LGN arrival precedes cortical arrival; no packet switches back to the left side after chiasm.
5. 27–32s, rule: A miniature left-half target representation settles inside the right cortical endpoint while both originating retinal paths remain distinct and connected. Why: The pathway groups information by visual hemifield, not by one eye per hemisphere. Visible result: One left visual hemifield is represented in right cortex using inputs from both eyes.

All on-screen labels and narration-equivalent captions are concise English. Use no spoken audio or music. Preserve the specific objects, state bindings and timing above. Render the registered composition for this slug and inspect the final MP4 at the stored risk moments.
Reproduction requires the packaged TSX source, the course kit, Remotion/React dependencies, Chromium and ffmpeg. This prompt describes the reviewed artifact; it is not a self-contained promise of pixel-identical reproduction without those files.
final_title: Visual Pathway: One Field, Two Retinal Routes
learning_objective: Follow left-hemifield information from both eyes to right visual cortex and distinguish nasal crossing from temporal noncrossing.
core_conclusion: Nasal retinal fibers cross at the optic chiasm; temporal retinal fibers stay on their side, so each visual hemifield reaches the opposite cortex.

requirement_prompt:
Create a 15-second silent educational animation in Manim Community Edition.

Explain “Visual pathway” using this visual metaphor: “a glowing neural circuit carrying one signal for Visual pathway”. Dynamically demonstrate the core formula or conclusion: The visual pathway carries retinal signals toward visual cortex..

Use one continuous scene and one clear narrative line. Explain only this concept; do not add comparisons, extensions, or side cases. Structure the motion in three connected beats:
1. 0–3 seconds: establish the objects, input, or initial state.
2. 3–10.95 seconds: show at least two causally connected state changes that reveal the mechanism and progressively connect key variables or conclusions to the visual.
3. 10.95–12.45 seconds: resolve the result, invariant, or central insight.

Keep introducing meaningful animation information until 12.45 seconds. Hold the final still frame for no more than 2.55 seconds.

All on-screen titles, labels, and supporting annotations must be short English phrases in Arial. Use a bright, non-black background (#EDF4FA); main visual (#154C79); secondary visual (#8A2D2D); highlight (#6B5700); and text (#172033). Maintain strong contrast and legibility.

Strict typography requirements:
- Render every complete title, label, phrase, or sentence as one native Text(...) object so every character shares one baseline.
- Never rebuild a line from separately positioned word or letter objects, and never align words by their individual bounding boxes.
- Create Arial text at a base font_size of 64, then uniformly scale the complete Text object to its final visual size; do not render explanatory text directly at a tiny font size.
- Preserve ordinary spaces inside the same Text object, set disable_ligatures=True, and do not add manual tracking, special-width spaces, or per-character offsets.

Use ThreeDScene for a genuinely spatial main visual: at least one core object must show volume, depth, or occlusion, and include one smooth camera move that reveals spatial structure. The 3D motion must clarify the concept rather than merely tilt a flat diagram. Render in 16:9.

Global rendering requirements:
- Never place plain English words, sentences, titles, or explanatory prose in MathTex, Tex, or inline LaTeX math mode. Use the native Text(...) component for all explanatory text and titles.
- If an English word is unavoidable inside a mathematical expression, explicitly wrap every word with \text{...}; never leave a word bare in algebra mode.
- Animate text at whole-word or whole-line granularity. Never split text into individually spaced letters or animate isolated letter spans.
- Do not use text-align: justify or the SVG textLength or lengthAdjust attributes.
- Use the final conclusion display as the video's opening poster frame; do not begin on an empty background.

production.scene_rationale: Five scenes are needed to disambiguate field-to-retina inversion, each eye’s optic nerve, selective chiasmal crossing, thalamic relay, and hemifield organization. The nine-second chiasm scene is longest because nasal crossing and temporal noncrossing must both be tracked.
